summary: This issue of Spatium (No. 5, June 2000), published by the Association Pro ISSI, is devoted to Earth, Moon and Mars and is based on a keynote address by Johannes Geiss at the Fourth Anniversary of the International Space Science Institute. It argues that comparative study of the three bodies illuminates planetary origins and evolution, covering the Giant Collision origin of the Moon, the Moon's geological history ending about 3,000 million years ago, and Mars's volcanoes, ancient rivers and possible traces of life. The note closes with an unresolved discussion of possible fossil life in Martian meteorites.
one_line: Spatium No. 5 (2000) surveys Earth, Moon and Mars, covering the Giant Collision origin of the Moon, lunar geology, Martian volcanoes and rivers, and possible life on Mars.
key_facts: Spatium No. 5 was published in June 2000 by the Association Pro ISSI and is devoted to Earth, Moon and Mars.
Johannes Geiss is the spiritus rector of the International Space Science Institute in Bern and its Executive Director.
The Sun was born 4,600 million years ago in a collapsing interstellar cloud.
The Giant Collision Theory was originally proposed by William K. Hartmann and colleagues in the United States.
The Giant Collision Theory explains that the Moon formed after a collision between Earth and another large object about ten percent of the Earth's mass.
Lunar rocks are completely free of crystalline water and hydrogen-containing minerals such as mica or clay minerals.
The Moon has much less iron relative to the Earth and meteorites, which would be expected if the giant impact occurred after the Earth formed its iron core.
Oxygen in terrestrial and lunar rocks has exactly the same isotopic composition.
Initially the tidal forces between Earth and Moon were more than a thousand times stronger than they are today.
The Moon's last major mare basalts ended not much later than 3,000 million years ago, after which the Moon has been geologically inactive.
The crater Copernicus was created by an impact about 900 million years ago.
Mars meteorites range in age from 4,500 to 150 million years.
The Sojourner vehicle was landed by NASA on the Martian surface on July 4, 1997.
Olympus Mons is higher and more massive than the highest mountains on Earth because Mars lacks plate tectonics.
Liquid water is a prerequisite for the emergence of life, at least the form of life we know.
